objective: By the end of this lesson you can say who has the right-of-way in any encounter under 14 CFR 91.113, what each pilot must do, and how to scan, use lights, and use ATC and ADS-B traffic without letting them replace your eyes.
why: Most midair collisions happen in good weather, in daylight, near airports [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. The rules give a clear answer to "who moves," but the real defense is a good scan, because traffic calls can come late or not at all [[16:14|AC 90-48E 16]] and displays do not show every aircraft [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]. AC 90-48E is the FAA guide to the pilot's side of this job [[16:1|AC 90-48E 1]].

prereading.what: The rules themselves: operating near other aircraft, formation, and every right-of-way case. Short; read every word.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.111 to 91.115

prereading.what: Why eyes miss traffic: refocus time, the 12.5 second reaction table, empty-field myopia, the blossom effect, haze and glare.
prereading.label: AC 90-48E 8.1

prereading.what: Typical collision cases, formation cautions, the scan pattern, blind spots, night scanning and why ATC and screens are not enough.
prereading.label: AC 90-48E 11 to 16

prereading.what: Vision in flight and the judgment side of collision avoidance: relative altitude, no relative motion, lights on.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-6 and 8-1-8

prereading.what: Visual separation, clearing procedures, ADS-B In best practices, TCAS and TIS limits.
prereading.label: AIM 4-4-14 to 4-4-17

prereading.what: Radar traffic information: what a traffic call contains, when you get it, and why the clock position can be off.
prereading.label: AIM 4-1-15

prereading.what: ADS-B Out and In, TIS-B, and their limits. Skim; focus on 4-5-7e and 4-5-8d.
prereading.label: AIM 4-5-7 and 4-5-8

warmup: Think first: You are cruising at 4,500 ft in a high-wing airplane. A low-wing airplane is converging from your left, a little above you, and your ADS-B display shows nothing. Who has the right-of-way, why might neither pilot see the other, and why is the display silent?

key_terms.def: Your legal duty, VFR or IFR, to watch for and stay clear of other aircraft whenever the weather lets you see them (91.113(b)).
Which aircraft may hold its path. The other pilot must give way.
Move so you stay clear. The pilot giving way may not pass over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft unless well clear.
An aircraft in serious trouble. It has the right-of-way over all other traffic.
Two aircraft closing at about the same altitude from the side, not head-on.
Catching up to an aircraft ahead. The one being overtaken has the right-of-way.
Flying close to another aircraft on purpose. Needs an arrangement with every PIC in the formation.
With nothing outside to focus on, the eyes relax and focus only 10 to 30 ft away. You look but do not see.
An aircraft on a collision course seems to sit still and stay small, then suddenly fills the windshield.
An ATC call about nearby traffic: clock position, distance, direction and type or altitude if known. Workload permitting.
Out: your airplane broadcasts its GPS position. In: your airplane receives and shows others. Out is required in some airspace; In is not.
Traffic sent from ATC radar to ADS-B In receivers. Shows only aircraft with transponders, and only where there is radar and ground station coverage.

chunks.title: See and avoid: the duty under every rule

callout.text: 91.113(b): when weather conditions permit, every pilot, IFR or VFR, must stay vigilant to see and avoid other aircraft. A pilot who must give way may not pass over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

body.p: Notice what the rule does not say. An IFR clearance does not end the duty. Neither does radar service. When an IFR flight is in VFR-on-top conditions, seeing and avoiding is the pilot's sole job [[33:282|AIM 4-4-11b]]. Terminal radar services for VFR pilots (TRSA, Class C and Class B service) do not relieve you of it either [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18e]]. AIM 5-5-8 puts it in one line: when weather permits, whatever the flight plan and whether or not under radar control, the pilot sees and avoids; the controller gives traffic information on a workload permitting basis [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]].

91.111(a) adds a plain rule: no one may fly so close to another aircraft that it creates a collision hazard [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(a)]]. Even if you have the right-of-way, yield if the other aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. The AIM says to know the right-of-way rules so that, if an aircraft is on an obvious collision course, you can take immediate evasive action, preferably within the rules [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8c]].

Most midair collisions and near misses happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport or near navigation aids [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. Busy places include airways near VORs and Class B, C, D and E surface areas [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: A nice day near your home airport is the most likely setting for a midair, not a bad one [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

check.q: You are IFR in clear air with ATC radar service. Who must see and avoid VFR traffic?
check.a: You do. The duty applies to IFR and VFR flights whenever weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

chunks.title: Who has the right-of-way: distress and aircraft category

callout.text: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]].

body.p: AC 90-48E gives a modern example. An airplane landing itself with an emergency autoland system is treated as in distress. If you hear its automatic radio message, be alert and give way [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.1]].
When aircraft of different categories converge, the category decides, not the side [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]:

head: This aircraft
Has the right-of-way over
rows: Any other category of aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)(1)]]
All other powered aircraft, except an aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)(3)]]
(d)(4) Aircraft towing or refueling other aircraft
Any other powered aircraft (the rule does not list airplanes or rotorcraft by name)
No category priority. Same category: the one on the right (next chunk) [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]

body.p: Two other groups must yield to you. An ultralight must yield the right-of-way to all aircraft [[60:729|14 CFR 103.13]]. A small unmanned aircraft (drone) must yield to all aircraft and may not pass over, under, or ahead unless well clear [[60:749|14 CFR 107.37]]. That does not end your duty to look: AC 90-48E asks pilots to stay vigilant for drones at or below 400 ft in uncontrolled airspace and at all times in VMC [[16:11|AC 90-48E 11.1.5]].

callout.text: Pecking order: distress, then balloon, glider, towing or refueling aircraft, airship, then other powered aircraft. Application: the rule lists airship before towing in (d)(3) and (d)(4), but (d)(4) puts towing or refueling aircraft over all other powered aircraft, airships included, so this ranking is a study aid built from 91.113(c) and (d) [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c), (d)]].

At non-towered fields, a glider, and its tow aircraft during towing, have the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.1]]. When gliders and airplanes share a runway, the glider pattern is inside the powered pattern [[17:16|AC 90-66C 12.2.2]].

check.q: You fly a Cessna. A glider converges from your left at your altitude. Who gives way?
check.a: You do. A glider has the right-of-way over powered aircraft, whatever side it is on [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].

head: Encounter
Who has the right-of-way
What the rule says to do
rows: Converging, same category, about the same altitude
The aircraft to the other's right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]
The other pilot gives way, passing well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]
Each pilot alters course to the right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]]
The overtaking pilot alters course to the right to pass well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]

body.p: Converging means "except head-on, or nearly so" [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. If you see the other airplane's right side, it is on your left and you have the right-of-way. If it is on your right, you give way.

callout.text: Every turn in these rules is a turn to the right: head-on, both go right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]]; overtaking, pass on the right [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]].

body.p: Overtaking matters more than it sounds. The AFH says a midair is most likely between two aircraft going the same direction [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. AC 90-48E lists head-on and overtaking in cruise as two typical midair setups [[16:11|AC 90-48E 11.1]].

Which way to move is your call. Climb, descend or turn is a judgment, but expect the other pilot to maneuver too. Watch the other aircraft during your maneuver, then start scanning again, since there may be others [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: Having the right-of-way gives no protection if the other pilot has not seen you. Yield if the other aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

check.q: You are catching a slower airplane on the same course and altitude. What does 91.113 require?
check.a: It has the right-of-way. You alter course to the right and pass well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]].

chunks.title: Landing right-of-way and the traffic pattern

callout.text: 91.113(g): aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way over aircraft in flight or on the surface. They may not use this to force off the runway an aircraft that has landed and is clearing for them. When two or more aircraft approach to land, the lower one has the right-of-way, but it may not use that to cut in front of an aircraft on final or to overtake it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

body.p: AC 90-66C repeats the rule for non-towered airports and reminds pilots that see and avoid applies all around the pattern [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]] [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.10]]. At a towered airport, ATC sequences you, for example with "report a 2 mile left base" [[16:11|AC 90-48E 11.1]].

The pattern is where many midairs happen. AFH Figure 8-4 shows final and the runway with the largest shares, 34 percent each, then downwind and short final at 16 percent each [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. The AFH also says nearly all of these occur at or near non-towered airports below 1,000 ft [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

bullets: Avoid entering the pattern while descending; it creates its own collision hazard [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].
Descend to pattern altitude before you enter the pattern [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Be aware some pattern traffic may have no radio, and use exterior lights to be seen [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
Before taking the runway, scan the approach area for landing traffic [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

check.q: Two airplanes are approaching to land, neither yet on final. One is 400 ft lower. Who has the right-of-way?
check.a: The lower one, but it may not use that to cut in front of an aircraft on final or to overtake it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

chunks.title: Operating near other aircraft and formation flight

callout.text: 91.111: (a) no one may fly so close to another aircraft that it creates a collision hazard; (b) formation flight only by arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft; (c) no formation flight while carrying passengers for hire [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111]].

body.p: AC 90-48E is blunt about formation. More recreational formation flights have meant more midairs between the formation aircraft. The FAA recommends training with an established formation training organization before you try it [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2]].

Maneuvering flight takes your eyes away from the scan. AC 90-48E says more than a quarter (26.6 percent) of fatal accidents over 10 years happened in maneuvering flight, which includes buzzing, formation, aerial work and aerobatics [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2]].

ATC can also put you near another aircraft on purpose. If you accept a call to follow traffic or keep visual separation, you agree to maneuver as needed to avoid it [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14b]]. Keep it in sight constantly and do not pass it until it is no longer a factor [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14]]. If you lose sight of it, tell the controller right away [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14]].

callout.text: "Let's fly together on the way" is formation flight. Agree on it before takeoff with the other PIC [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(b)]], and never with paying passengers on board [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(c)]].

check.q: A friend suggests a loose two-ship to the fly-in. You have not discussed it. What does 91.111 require first?
check.a: An arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft in the formation [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(b)]]. With passengers for hire on board it is not allowed at all [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(c)]].

body.p: Detection depends on six things: image size, brightness, contrast, how well your eyes have adapted, motion, and how long the object is in view [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1]]. Several of them work against you.

bullets: Refocusing: it takes 1 to 2 seconds to refocus from a panel 2 ft away to an aircraft 1 mile away [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]].

Narrow focus: the eyes take in nearly 200 degrees but classify an object only within about 10 to 15 degrees [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]]. An aircraft 7 miles away seen in sharp central vision would have to be within 7/10 of a mile to be recognized off center [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Empty-field myopia: above clouds or in a haze layer, with nothing outside to focus on, the eyes relax to a focal distance of 10 to 30 ft [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].
Binocular vision: a windshield post can hide a target from one eye. Move your head, not just your eyes [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]].
Blossom effect: an aircraft on a collision course seems to sit still and stay small, then suddenly fills the window. A bug smear can hide it [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]].

Haze and glare: on a hazy day traffic is hard to see even with 5 sm visibility, and flying into the sun hides aircraft. The AC recommends flying above haze and keeping the windshield clean [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9 to 8.1.10]].

head: Event (AC 90-48E Table 1)
Seconds
rows: Decision to turn left or right
Total before the aircraft begins to move

body.p: The AC says the table uses Transportation Safety Board of Canada data that draw on U.S. Naval Aviation Safety Center reaction times [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. Add a 1 to 2 second refocus and the margin shrinks again [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]].

callout.text: An aircraft with no relative motion that stays in one part of your windshield is likely on a collision course. If it shows no sideways or vertical motion but grows, take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

check.q: Why is a target with no relative motion so dangerous?
check.a: It is likely on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]], and the eye needs motion or contrast to notice it, so it may "blossom" late [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]].

chunks.title: How to scan and clear blind spots

callout.text: Scan in short, regular eye movements. Each one no more than 10 degrees, and look at each area for at least 1 second [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Pick a pattern that suits you and stick to it [[16:12|AC 90-48E 12]].

body.p: Time inside should be no more than 1/4 to 1/3 of the time outside: about 4 to 5 seconds on the panel for every 16 seconds outside [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. The AIM suggests starting over the left shoulder and moving right, coming back inside along the right wing [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Studying charts and setting up frequencies before flight frees up scan time [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

High-wing airplanes cannot see well above; low-wing airplanes cannot see well below. The worst case is a low-wing airplane above a high-wing airplane [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Door posts and wings make more blind spots: move your head, and at times lift a wing to see [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8j]]. Windshield posts, sun visors and the airplane's attitude add others [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

bullets: Before a turn: a high-wing pilot raises the wing toward the turn and looks; a low-wing pilot lowers it and looks [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]].
Climbs and descents: make gentle banks left and right so you can keep scanning [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]. In a climb, adjust the pitch attitude so you can see over the nose [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Long straight and level legs: break them up at intervals with clearing procedures [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15c]].
Look behind now and then, from behind the right wing across to the left wing [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Relative altitude: a target above the horizon is probably higher than you; below it, probably lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

callout.text: Call it out loud: "clear left, right, above, below." The AIM asks training programs to have pilots verbalize clearing [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

check.q: Which pairing hides each airplane from the other worst?
check.a: A low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing airplane [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

callout.text: From sunset to sunrise, no one may operate an aircraft without lighted position lights. An aircraft equipped with an anticollision light system must have those lights lit, day or night, but the PIC may turn them off when operating conditions make that in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]].

body.p: Position lights are red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, white on the tail [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. They tell you which way another airplane is going. Red on the left and green on the right means it is going your way. Red on the right and green on the left means it is coming toward you and could be on a collision course [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

Operation Lights On is a voluntary FAA program. Turn on landing lights for takeoff, and below 10,000 ft day or night, especially within 10 miles of an airport, in low visibility, and where birds gather [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. Exterior lights greatly increase how easily you are seen, day or night [[34:189|AIM 8-1-8k, l]]. AC 90-48E's "Lights, Camera, Action" before takeoff: lights on, transponder on, call sign stated [[16:10|AC 90-48E 10.4.1]].

At night, the center of your vision has a blind spot 5 to 10 degrees wide. Look about 10 degrees above, below or beside a dim object, and pause a few seconds in each part of the scan [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]]. Ground lights make other aircraft harder to pick out [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].

callout.text: Lights help others see you, but not every aircraft has them on. Keep your scan going [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

check.q: At night you see another airplane's green light on its left and red light on its right. What does that tell you?
check.a: It is coming toward you and could be on a collision course [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

chunks.title: ATC traffic advisories: what they are and what they miss

body.p: Radar traffic information tells you about a target that may pass close enough to need your attention. It does not relieve you of continual vigilance to see and avoid [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]]. IFR flights get it routinely; VFR flights may get it when they ask [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]].

A traffic call gives the clock position, distance in NM, direction of travel, and type and altitude if known [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15c]]. Altitude needs Mode C and a facility that can show it [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]]. VFR advisories do not include vectors away from traffic unless you ask [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]].

The controller sees only your track, not your heading. If you are crabbing for wind, the traffic will not be where the clock call says. In AIM FIG 4-1-1, both pilots are told "12 o'clock." Pilot A sees it at 2 o'clock and pilot B at 10 o'clock [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].

callout.text: The service is workload permitting. Radar limits, traffic volume and frequency congestion can stop it, the controller has complete discretion, and the controller need not tell you why [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]]. AC 90-48E: do not depend only on ATC traffic advisories [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15 and 16]].

body.p: If you are under ATC control and the controller is aware of another aircraft, not under their control, in unsafe proximity to you, you get an immediate traffic alert, with its position if time permits and, when feasible, an alternate course of action [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16b]]. Once an alert is issued, what to do is solely your decision [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]].

check.q: You are holding a left crab for wind and ATC calls traffic at 12 o'clock. Where do you look first?
check.a: To the right of the nose. In AIM FIG 4-1-1, pilot A, crabbing like this, sees "12 o'clock" traffic at 2 o'clock [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].

chunks.title: ADS-B In, TIS-B and TCAS: aids, not eyes

body.p: ADS-B Out is your airplane broadcasting its position; ADS-B In is receiving others [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a]]. Aircraft in the airspace listed in 91.225 must have ADS-B Out [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a]], for example Class A [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]], Class B and C, and Class E in the 48 states at and above 10,000 ft MSL, excluding 2,500 ft AGL and below [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(b), (d)]]. The regulations do not require ADS-B In [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a]].

callout.text: An ADS-B traffic display is not a collision avoidance system and does not relieve you of see and avoid. Do not maneuver on it in IMC or without seeing the intruder. It only helps you find traffic visually [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]].

bullets: Not everything shows. In some airspace aircraft have no ADS-B Out or transponder and will not appear [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]].

TIS-B relays only transponder-equipped targets, and only where there is radar coverage [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8]]. Its updates come every 3 to 13 seconds, versus about once per second for ADS-B, and nothing tells you if you are outside its coverage [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].
If IFR, do not deviate from a clearance for a TIS-B target without ATC approval unless there is an imminent emergency [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].
TIS and TCAS I give proximity warnings only; no avoidance maneuver is recommended or authorized from them [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].

TCAS II resolution advisories: respond at once unless unsafe, and tell ATC [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]]. 91.123 lets you deviate from a clearance for an RA but you must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].

callout.text: "Traffic in sight" must mean you see it out the window, not on the screen [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]].

body.p: Screens can also pull your eyes inside. AC 90-48E warns that new systems can cause fixation on the displays [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15 and 16]]. Best use: fold the display into your normal scan, use its alerts, limit time on tablets, and scan the whole sky [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]]. NTSB studies cited in the AC concluded that the ADS-B Traffic Advisory System (ATAS) would have given 30 to 39 seconds of warning in the Ketchikan midair [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.2]].

check.q: Your display shows no traffic near a small non-towered airport. Can you assume the pattern is empty?
check.a: No. Aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder will not show [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]], and TIS-B needs radar coverage [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8]].

bullets: Holding course because "I have the right-of-way" while the other pilot has not seen you. Fix: yield if it is too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Turning left in a head-on. Fix: both turn right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]].
Passing ahead of an aircraft you must give way to. Fix: pass behind or well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].
Cutting in front of an airplane on final because you are lower. Fix: the lower aircraft may not do that [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].
Answering "traffic in sight" from the screen. Fix: only when you see it out the window [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]].
Trusting an empty display. Fix: many aircraft are not shown [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]].
Looking where the controller says and stopping there. Fix: allow for your crab angle [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].
Long heads-down periods. Fix: about 4 to 5 seconds inside for every 16 outside [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

check.q: Why should a pilot with the right-of-way still be ready to move?
check.a: The other pilot may not have seen them; yield if the other aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]], and take evasive action when a collision is near [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

scenario.title: The fly-in on a hazy Saturday
scenario.setup: You fly a low-wing Piper Cherokee to a fly-in at a non-towered field 60 NM away. It is a hazy summer afternoon with about 6 sm visibility, and your route heads west into the sun. A friend in a Cessna 172 calls you before departure: "Let's fly over together." You have VFR flight following and a portable ADS-B In receiver on a tablet. A glider operation is near the destination.

questions.q: Your friend wants to join up "loosely" on the way. What must happen first, and what does the FAA recommend?
questions.a: Formation flight is allowed only by arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft, and never with passengers for hire [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111]]. AC 90-48E links rising formation flying to more midairs and recommends training with a formation training organization first [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2]].

questions.q: How do the haze and the sun affect your scan, and what can you do?
questions.a: Haze makes traffic hard to see even with legal visibility, and flying into the sun hides aircraft [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9 to 8.1.10]]. Fly above the haze if you can, keep the windshield clean [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9 to 8.1.10]], and use lights to be seen [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

questions.q: Where are your Cherokee's blind spots, and how do you clear them before the descent?
questions.a: Low-wing airplanes see poorly below, and the worst case is you above a high-wing airplane [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. Make gentle banks left and right during the descent, and lower the wing toward a turn and look before turning [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]] [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

questions.q: Center gave you three traffic calls, then went quiet on a busy frequency. Your tablet shows nothing nearby. Are you covered?
questions.a: No. Advisories are workload permitting and can stop without notice [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]], and the AC says not to depend only on them [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15 and 16]]. The display misses aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]]. Keep scanning.

questions.q: Near the field a glider converges from your left at your altitude. Who gives way, and how?
questions.a: You do. A glider has the right-of-way over powered aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. Give way without passing over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

questions.q: On a 45 degree entry you see your friend's 172 on final, lower than you, and an RV on downwind ahead. Who lands first, and what must you not do?
questions.a: The airplane on final has the right-of-way [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Follow the traffic already in the pattern; do not cut in front of an airplane on final or overtake it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. If you overtake anyone, pass on the right and well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]].

skills.do: Given an encounter (the other aircraft's category, its position, and the phase of flight), say who has the right-of-way under 91.113, what each pilot must do, and how you would spot the traffic and keep watching it.
skills.practice: Make a stack of cards, one per case: distress, each category pair, converging from left and right, head-on, overtaking, two aircraft approaching to land [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]] [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Say the rule and the action aloud. On your next flight, verbalize "clear left, right, above, below" before each turn [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]], and practice spotting called traffic out the window before looking at the screen [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]].

quiz.q: When does the 91.113(b) see-and-avoid duty apply?
options: When weather conditions permit, regardless of IFR or VFR operation
Only to VFR flights, since IFR flights are separated by ATC
Only outside Class B and C airspace, where ATC provides separation
Only when you are not receiving radar services from ATC
quiz.why: "When weather conditions permit, regardless of whether an operation is conducted under" IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

quiz.q: Which aircraft has the right-of-way over all other air traffic?
options: An aircraft in distress
An aircraft on final
An aircraft towing a glider
A balloon
quiz.why: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]].

quiz.q: The 91.113(d) rule for two converging aircraft of the same category applies when they are:
options: At approximately the same altitude, except head-on or nearly so
At any altitude within about 1 NM of each other, except head-on or nearly so
Only when they are meeting head-on or nearly so at the same altitude
Only when both are in the traffic pattern at an airport at the same time
quiz.why: The converging rule covers aircraft of the same category converging at approximately the same altitude, except head-on or nearly so [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].

quiz.q: You fly a Bonanza. An airship converges from your left at your altitude. Who gives way?
options: The airship, because you are on its right
Both turn right
You, because an airship has the right-of-way over all other powered aircraft except one towing or refueling
Neither; it is a different category
quiz.why: An airship has the right-of-way over all other powered aircraft, except an aircraft towing or refueling [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].

options: Only with an FAA waiver
By arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft, and never carrying passengers for hire
Anytime the pilots can see each other
Only in Class G airspace
quiz.why: Formation flight needs an arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(b)]], and no one may fly formation carrying passengers for hire [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(c)]].

quiz.q: For an effective scan, each eye movement should be no more than ___ and each area looked at for at least ___.
options: 30 degrees; 1/2 second
10 degrees; 3 seconds
20 degrees; 2 seconds
10 degrees; 1 second
quiz.why: Each movement should not exceed 10 degrees, and each area should be observed for at least 1 second [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]].

quiz.q: Which pairing is the worst case for blind spots?
options: A low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing airplane
Two high-wing airplanes flying side by side at the same altitude
A high-wing airplane flying above a low-wing airplane
Two low-wing airplanes meeting head-on at the same altitude
quiz.why: High-wing airplanes see poorly above and low-wing airplanes below, so a low-wing above a high-wing is the worst case [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

quiz.q: ADS-B Out is required in Class B. What about ADS-B In?
options: Required in the same airspace
Required only above 10,000 ft MSL
Not required by the regulations
Required for all VFR flights since 2020
quiz.why: 91.225 requires ADS-B Out in listed airspace; the AIM notes the regulations do not require ADS-B In [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a]].

quiz.q: Compared with ADS-B, which updates about once per second, how often do TIS-B traffic updates arrive?
options: About once every minute
About once every second, the same as ADS-B
About once every 30 seconds
About once every 3 to 13 seconds
quiz.why: TIS-B updates come less often than ADS-B, approximately once every 3 to 13 seconds depending on the radar in use; ADS-B is nominally once per second [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8d]].

final_quiz.q: You and a Bonanza are both approaching the same airport to land, neither on final yet. The Bonanza is 500 ft below you. Who has the right-of-way?
options: You, because you were there first
The Bonanza, because it is lower
Neither; use the converging rule
Whoever is faster
final_quiz.why: When two or more aircraft are approaching to land, the lower one has the right-of-way [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. It still may not cut in front of an aircraft on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

final_quiz.q: You have just landed and are rolling to the first taxiway. An airplane is on short final behind you. What does 91.113(g) say about it?
options: It must go around because you are on the runway
You have the right-of-way because you landed first
It has the right-of-way but may not use that to force you off the runway while you make way
ATC must decide at any airport
final_quiz.why: Landing aircraft have the right-of-way, but may not use the rule to force off the runway an aircraft that has landed and is making way [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

final_quiz.q: A small drone hovers at 300 ft AGL near your path in Class G. Who must yield, and what is still your job?
options: You must yield, because small drones have the right-of-way over you in Class G
Neither; drones are not covered by any right-of-way rule, so you need not look for them
The drone yields only if it is converging from your left, as with any aircraft
The drone must yield to all aircraft, but you still must see and avoid
final_quiz.why: A small unmanned aircraft must yield the right-of-way to all aircraft [[60:749|14 CFR 107.37]]. Your see-and-avoid duty remains [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and AC 90-48E asks pilots to stay vigilant for drones at or below 400 ft in uncontrolled airspace [[16:11|AC 90-48E 11.1.5]].

final_quiz.q: Approach asks you to maintain visual separation from a Cessna ahead, and you accept. A minute later you lose sight of it in the haze. What should you do?
options: Tell the controller promptly that you lost sight of it
Nothing, because ATC is still responsible for separating you from it
Keep going on course and look for it again in a minute or so
Turn off your transponder so the controller's screen clears of clutter
final_quiz.why: Accepting visual separation means you maneuver to avoid the other aircraft; if you lose visual contact, promptly tell the controller [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14]].

final_quiz.q: At night, another airplane at your altitude shows a red light on its right side and a green light on its left. What is happening?
options: It is flying the same direction as you, ahead and slightly to one side
It is climbing away from you and the two courses are diverging
It is turning away from you toward a different heading
It is heading toward you and could be on a collision course
final_quiz.why: Red on the right and green on the left means it could be on a collision course; red left and green right means it is going your way [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

final_quiz.q: IFR in cloud, your ADS-B display shows a target 1 NM ahead at your altitude. ATC has said nothing. What should you do?
options: Do not maneuver on the display alone; ask ATC about the traffic
Turn away right now based on the display, since ADS-B shows exact position
Climb 500 ft right away to get above it, then tell ATC what you did
Ignore it completely, since traffic displays are never accurate enough to use
final_quiz.why: ADS-B must not be used for avoidance maneuvers in IMC or without visual contact [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7e]]. For TIS-B traffic the AIM adds that any deviation from a clearance needs ATC approval first unless there is an imminent emergency [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has TCAS I and you get a traffic advisory. What is the correct use?
options: Fly the climb or descent it commands
Turn right, as in a head-on
Report "traffic in sight" to ATC
Use it to find the traffic visually; no avoidance maneuver comes from TCAS I
final_quiz.why: TCAS I gives proximity warning only, to help visual acquisition. No avoidance maneuvers are recommended or authorized from it [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].

final_quiz.q: Another airplane stays in the same spot on your windshield and slowly gets bigger. What does the AIM say?
options: It is at a much higher altitude and will pass safely overhead
It is moving away from you and will soon disappear from view
It is likely on a collision course; take evasive action
It is a reflection of your own aircraft in the windshield glass
final_quiz.why: No relative motion means a likely collision course, and if it grows with no lateral or vertical motion, take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: On VFR flight following, the controller stops calling traffic and does not say why. Is that allowed?
options: No, once started it must continue
Yes, the controller has complete discretion and need not give a reason
Only in Class A airspace
No, the controller must tell you why
final_quiz.why: Controllers have complete discretion to provide or continue the service, and the reason need not be given [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]].

final_quiz.q: On frequency you hear an automated voice say an airplane is landing itself at your airport. How do you treat it?
options: Normal traffic; converging rules apply
Ask it to change runways
It must give way because it has no pilot
As in distress: be alert and give way
final_quiz.why: The FAA treats aircraft under emergency autoland as in distress, with the right-of-way over all others; give way [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14.1]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]].

final_quiz.q: A friend wants you to fly formation with him on a paid sightseeing flight with two paying passengers in your airplane. Under 91.111:
options: Legal, as long as both PICs agree on the formation arrangement first
Legal if you stay below 1,000 ft AGL and away from congested areas
Not allowed: no formation flight carrying passengers for hire
Legal if ATC approves the formation and both airplanes are on a flight plan
final_quiz.why: No person may operate an aircraft carrying passengers for hire in formation flight [[60:447|14 CFR 91.111(c)]].

final_quiz.q: A hazy summer day with 5 sm visibility. What does AC 90-48E recommend for seeing traffic?
options: Fly in the haze, since 5 sm is legal VFR and needs no extra care
Fly above the haze layer and keep the windshield clean
Turn off exterior lights to reduce glare off the haze at all times
Fly directly into the sun for better contrast against traffic
final_quiz.why: Hazy days make traffic hard to see, so the AC recommends flying above haze and keeping windshields clean [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9 to 8.1.10]].

final_quiz.q: Your anticollision strobes are reflecting badly off the clouds at night. May you turn them off?
options: Yes, the PIC may turn them off in the interest of safety
Only with ATC approval, since the lights are required equipment
Only if the position lights are turned off at the same time
No, they must be on whenever equipped and the engine is running
final_quiz.why: Anticollision lights need not be lit when the PIC determines that turning them off is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]]. The AIM adds that supplementary strobe lights should be turned off in flight when there is adverse reflection from clouds [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24a]].

takeaways: See and avoid applies IFR and VFR whenever weather permits; radar and screens never remove it.
Distress first, then balloon, glider, towing or refueling aircraft, airship, then the rest; same category, the one on the right.
Head-on: both turn right. Overtaking: the overtaken has the right-of-way; pass on the right, well clear.
Landing: aircraft on final have the right-of-way; lower has priority, but never cut in front.
Formation only by arrangement with every PIC, never with passengers for hire.
Scan in 10 degree steps, 1 second each, mostly outside; clear blind spots with banks and head moves.
Traffic calls and ADS-B help you find traffic; only your eyes clear it.
cfi_notes: PHAK Figure 14-44 says pilot A sees the "12 o'clock" traffic at 1 o'clock [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]]. AIM FIG 4-1-1, the same layout, says 2 o'clock [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]]. Both agree that pilot B sees it at 10 o'clock and that the call is based on track. This lesson uses the AIM numbers.

AIM 4-4-14d cites "14 CFR section 91.113(a)" for the duty to see and avoid [[33:286|AIM 4-4-14d]]. In the current CFR text, 91.113(a) says the section does not apply on water, and the see-and-avoid wording is in 91.113(b) [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(a), (b)]]. AIM 4-5-8d cites "91.113b" [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8d]], and AC 90-66C quotes the (b) wording under "91.113" [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]].

AFH 1-10 says the see-and-avoid concept requires vigilance "at all times" [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. The CFR text reads "when weather conditions permit" [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Teach the CFR wording. Application: in practice, look whenever you can see out.

AC 90-48E paragraph 14, a list of recommended equipment, includes "the ADS-B In and display capability, required as of January 1, 2020" [[16:14|AC 90-48E 14]], which can read as if ADS-B In were required. The same AC, paragraph 7.1, describes the ADS-B requirement by airspace and points to 91.225 [[16:4|AC 90-48E 7.1]]. 91.225 requires ADS-B Out equipment after January 1, 2020 in listed airspace [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]], and AIM 4-5-7a says the regulations do not require ADS-B In [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a]]. Teach the CFR and AIM.

The source note under 91.113 lists amendments through Amdt. 91-379 (Nov. 21, 2024) and Amdt. 91-381 (July 24, 2025) [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113]]. The sources do not show the earlier wording or what each amendment changed. Teach the category list as printed now: (d)(1) to (d)(4) speak of "powered aircraft" and do not name airplanes, rotorcraft or other classes [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]].
AFH 8-6 statistics (time of day percentages, Figure 8-4) carry no date or data source on the page [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. Use them to show where to look hardest, not as current numbers.

Application: ride along with the pilot's eyes. Call traffic you see before they do, and count heads-down seconds against the AIM 4 to 5 seconds per 16 [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. AC 90-48E asks instructors to guard against their own preoccupation during instruction [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].
For pilots with ADS-B In, ask them to show how their unit alerts, then ask what it cannot show (non-transponder aircraft, gaps in TIS-B coverage) [[33:306|AIM 4-5-8d]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]].

Interpretation: 91.113 does not define "approximately the same altitude" or "head-on, or nearly so" [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d), (e)]]. Application: when in doubt, treat it as head-on and turn right; and even with the right-of-way, yield if the other aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
gaps: AC 90-48E mentions the ADS-B Traffic Advisory System (ATAS) and how to request it and points to the Chart Users' Guide, but neither the AIM nor the Chart Users' Guide in the sources describes ATAS, so its details are not taught.
Each airplane's blind spots and each ADS-B In unit's alerts and settings come from the POH or AFM supplement and the avionics guide, not from these sources.
Formation flying technique is not in the sources; AC 90-48E points to an AOPA article and formation training organizations.
91.115 (water operations) is for seaplanes and is only mentioned here [[60:448|14 CFR 91.115]].

activities.title: True or false: see and avoid
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An IFR flight in clear air must still see and avoid other aircraft.
cards.why: True. The duty applies IFR or VFR when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

cards.s: If you have the right-of-way, you should hold course no matter how close the other aircraft gets.
cards.why: False. Yield if another aircraft seems too close [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]], and take evasive action when a collision is near [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

cards.s: The pilot who must give way may pass over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft if well clear.
cards.why: True. The rule bars passing over, under, or ahead "unless well clear" [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

cards.s: It is fine to enter the traffic pattern while still descending to pattern altitude.
cards.why: False. Entries into the pattern while descending create specific collision hazards and should be avoided [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15d]]. Descend to pattern altitude before entering [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

cards.s: Being in a radar environment means you can relax your scan.
cards.why: False. Most collisions happen on good weather days, and a radar environment still needs vigilance [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

cards.s: No one may fly so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.

activities.title: Who gives way?
activities.intro: You fly a Cessna 172 at cruise. Tap each encounter, then tap who must give way.
buckets: Both alter course to the right

items.t: A Piper converging from your right at your altitude
A Piper converging from your left at your altitude
A Bonanza coming straight at you, nose to nose
You are catching a slower Cub ahead on the same course
A faster Mooney is catching you from behind
A hot air balloon drifting toward your path
An airplane towing a glider, converging from your left
A powered ultralight converging from your right

activities.why: Same category: the one on the right has the right-of-way [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. Head-on: both turn right [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(e)]]. Overtaking: the overtaken has it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]. Balloons and towing aircraft rank above you [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. Ultralights yield to all aircraft [[60:729|14 CFR 103.13]].

activities.title: Limits of the eye
activities.intro: Tap a limitation, then what it means.

pairs.r: Eyes relax to focus 10 to 30 ft away
Target seems still, then suddenly fills the window
Objects classified only within about 10 to 15 degrees
1 to 2 seconds from panel to a distant aircraft
A post hides the target from one eye; move your head
5 to 10 degrees wide; look about 10 degrees off

activities.why: Empty-field myopia [[34:187|AIM 8-1-6c]]. Blossom effect, narrow focus and binocular vision [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.4 to 8.1.8]]. Refocus time [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1]]. Night blind spot [[16:13|AC 90-48E 13.1]].

activities.title: From seeing to swerving
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the events of AC 90-48E Table 1 in order, then tap Check.
steps: Decision to turn left or right
activities.why: AC 90-48E Table 1 lists these steps, adding up to 12.5 seconds before the airplane begins to move [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]].

activities.title: How much time do you have?
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Two airplanes fly head-on at 140 and 160 knots. Using the AC 90-48E total of 12.5 seconds before an airplane begins to move, how many NM do they close in that time? (2 decimals)
items.why: Closure 140 + 160 = 300 kt. 300 x 12.5 / 3,600 = 1.04 NM [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. Application: if you first see them inside about a mile, the reaction time alone is used up.

items.q: Using AC 90-48E Table 1, how many seconds pass from "see object" through "decision to turn left or right"?
Two airplanes are 1.5 NM apart head-on, at 110 and 130 knots. How many seconds until they meet if nobody turns?
items.why: Closure 110 + 130 = 240 kt. 1.5 x 3,600 / 240 = 22.5 seconds. Subtract the 12.5 second reaction total [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]] and only 10 seconds remain to spot them.

items.q: Using the upper AIM figure of 5 seconds inside for every 16 seconds outside, what is the most time inside the cockpit during 48 seconds of looking outside?

activities.title: Read the position lights
activities.intro: Drag each label to its pin on the airplane.
activities.why: Red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, white on the tail [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

activities.title: Traffic, two o'clock: a flight that unfolds
activities.intro: You fly a Cessna 172 VFR with flight following at 5,500 ft, crabbing left into a wind from your left. You have an ADS-B In display. You are 20 NM from a non-towered destination.

steps.s: Approach calls: "Traffic 12 o'clock, 4 miles, eastbound, altitude unknown." Your display shows a target there. What do you say and do?
options: Reply "Traffic in sight" because the target is clearly shown on your traffic display
Ask for a vector right away and then stop looking, since ATC will separate you
"Looking," then search outside, starting where the call and your crab suggest
Say nothing, since VFR advisories are optional and you are not required to reply
steps.why: "Traffic in sight" must mean seen out the window [[33:288|AIM 4-4-17]]. VFR advisories do not include vectors unless you ask [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b]].

steps.s: Your nose points left of your track. Where should you look for "12 o'clock" traffic?
options: To the right of the nose
To the left of the nose
Exactly over the nose
Behind the left wing
steps.why: ATC sees only your track. In AIM FIG 4-1-1, pilot A, crabbed like you, sees "12 o'clock" traffic at 2 o'clock [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]].

steps.s: You spot it: a low-wing airplane converging from your right at your altitude, no relative motion, slowly growing. What now?
options: Hold course and speed; you are on its left, so you have the right-of-way
Turn left to cross in front of it so that you clear its path first
Climb right away and pass directly over it, since it is a low-wing type
Give way: turn so you pass behind it, well clear, and keep watching it
steps.why: The aircraft on the right has the right-of-way [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(d)]]. Do not pass over, under, or ahead unless well clear [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. No relative motion means a likely collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

steps.s: Approach terminates service near the field. The display shows no traffic around the airport. How do you join the pattern?
options: Descend to pattern altitude before entering, announce, and scan the pattern and final
Fly a straight-in descending approach straight to the runway, since the display is empty
Enter the pattern while still descending from cruise altitude to save time
Skip the radio calls and pattern scan, since nobody is there on the display
steps.why: Aircraft without ADS-B Out or a transponder will not show [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15f, g]]. Avoid descending pattern entries [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]; descend to pattern altitude first and keep a visual scan [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

steps.s: Turning base, you see a Cub on a long straight-in final, lower than you. Who goes first?
options: You, because you are already established in the pattern and turning base ahead of it
The Cub; aircraft on final have the right-of-way, so extend and follow it
Whoever can reach the runway threshold first, as at a busy tower field
The faster airplane, because it can clear the runway for the other
steps.why: Aircraft on final have the right-of-way over others in flight [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Final and the runway are where the most pattern midairs happen [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
